To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the leaching behaviour of the fly ash waste is controlled by the precipitation and dissolution of a large number of different minerals.

(1) the complex dissolution and reprecipitation of heavy metals in high saline solutions can be modelled successfully with the program code EQ 3/6 and (2) the concentrations of zinc and cadmium in the leachate are limited by the precipitation of the hydroxides and carbonates of these elements.
the leachate concentrations of heavy metals from fly ashes can be reduced to a very small fraction of their initial values, if the fly ashes are stored in high saline solutions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the chemical equilibrium composition of the resulting leachates from a fly ash waste and the chemical processes involved.
the complex reactions between toxic chemical wastes and high saline solutions, which are of importance for the safety assessment of a repository for toxic chemical waste in salt formations.
the chemical equilibrium compositions in the complex systems of high saline solutions and chemical wastes, and the resulting geochemical modelling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the investigated reactions are of minor importance in the context of an underground repository for toxic wastes.
the complex reactions between high-saline solutions and chemical toxic wastes are not as severe as previously thought.
in the case of the investigated fly ash the maximum leaching concentrations of zinc and cadmium into a saline leachate are well below the limits for drinking water.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in a repository in salt formations, the leaching of toxic chemical wastes is strongly influenced by the presence of high concentrations of dissolved salts.
the leaching of heavy metals from toxic wastes into saline solutions is strongly dependent on the composition of these solutions.
the complex reactions between high-saline solutions and toxic chemical waste can be described by a geochemical equilibrium model.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the chemical equilibrium compositions can be determined experimentally and modelled with a reasonable degree of accuracy.
geochemical modelling is an appropriate tool to predict the leaching behaviour of toxic wastes in underground repositories.
the leachability of the heavy metals zinc and cadmium from the investigated waste is not significantly affected by the addition of high saline solutions.
